meta.title: Data Analysis for Business, Economics, and Policy: a tour for instructors
meta.author: Gábor Békés

slides.speaker: Who this is for: instructors deciding whether to adopt the book, or which parts to use.

blocks.content: Data Analysis for Business, Economics, and Policy
Gábor Békés and Gábor Kézdi
Cambridge University Press, 2021
A short tour for instructors thinking about using the book

slides.speaker: Cleaning and organizing affect the result as much as any other step. The book follows this whole process, not just the estimation step.

blocks.content: Data analysis is a process

items.content: Start with a question
Collect data, or check whether the data we have can answer it
Clean and organize the data
Explore it to learn the context
Pick a method, run it, check robustness
Interpret, visualize, and answer the question

slides.speaker: This is the main reason the book exists. The rest of the deck shows how it does it.

blocks.content: Methods textbooks rarely teach the project
Econometrics and data science textbooks are often excellent at teaching methods. But they say little about how to carry out an actual analysis from beginning to end.
Students learn that from projects, advisors and peers. We wanted a textbook that teaches it, too.

slides.speaker: We selected the most widely used methods that tend to work well, so each one gets a detailed treatment and we can compare them, in general and in the case studies.

blocks.content: Four parts, 24 chapters

rows: Data collection and quality, wrangling, EDA and visualization, generalizing, testing
Non-parametric and linear models, functional form, validity, probability models, time series
Loss functions, cross-validation, LASSO, trees, random forest, boosting, classification, forecasting
Potential outcomes and DAGs, experiments, matching, diff-in-diffs, panel methods, synthetic control, event studies

slides.speaker: Every case study also discusses data quality, exploratory analysis, interpretation, and internal and external validity. They are much more than illustrations of a method.

blocks.content: 47 case studies, one third of the book

items.content: Each starts with a real question and ends with an answer
Real data, messy and complicated, cleaned along the way
Topics: consumer decisions, policy, finance, management, health, sport
One third from the US, one third from Europe and the UK, one third from elsewhere

slides.speaker: This is the clearest example of the process idea: the same data, the same question, and a new method each time it comes back.

blocks.content: One question runs through seven case studies
*Which hotels in Vienna are underpriced relative to location and quality?*

rows: Collect the data by web scraping
Prepare it: tidy table, missing values, duplicates
Explore distributions, decide about extreme values
Simple regression, then non-linear functional forms
Check how stable the price–distance pattern is
Multiple regression to find the good deals

slides.speaker: Pick the ones closest to your students' interests. Each has data and code.

blocks.content: The other case studies travel widely

items.content: Gender and age differences in earnings (USA)
Management quality and firm size (Mexico, international)
Predicting firm exit with machine learning (EU)
Working from home and employee performance (China)
Airline mergers and prices (USA)
Replacing football team managers (UK)

blocks.content: All 47: [gabors-data-analysis.com/casestudies](https://gabors-data-analysis.com/casestudies/)

slides.speaker: Understanding the formulas is not required to learn from the book, but we encourage students to work with them.

blocks.content: Formulas, explained in plain English
Every formula is explained in words when it is introduced, and again when a case study uses it.
The math needed is basic calculus. Some matrix algebra and probability help, and we cover what is needed.
Derivations and extras sit in *Under the Hood* sections, so instructors can choose the depth.

slides.speaker: No programming experience is needed to start; students can learn coding during the course.

blocks.content: Everything is reproducible, in R, Python and Stata

items.content: Raw and clean data for every case study, on OSF
Code that cleans the data and produces every table and graph, on GitHub
Same results in three languages, so students can compare solutions
Coding courses that take students from zero to the case studies

slides.speaker: 24 chapters fit a 25–30 week academic year almost one chapter per week. Undergraduate programs often spread the book over two years: Parts I–II, then III–IV. For PhD students, Part IV pairs well with Angrist and Pischke.

slides.speaker: The book is written for self-study, which frees contact time. Multiple choice questions from the publisher work as start-of-class quizzes.

blocks.content: Three teaching habits that worked for us

items.content: **Assign reading in advance.** Run a short quiz at the start, then spend class on questions and case studies.
**Run code in class.** Students like seeing the sausage in the making, and then tinker on their own.
**Make students replicate.** Each chapter ends with data exercises. Start from the case study code, change one thing.
